unit.title: Inequalities & Constraints
unit.essential_question: How do inequalities represent ranges, limits, choices, and constraints—and how can we verify that a solution set fits both the mathematics and the situation?
big_ideas: An inequality compares quantities without requiring them to be equal.
A solution set may contain many values and can be represented with symbols, words, tables, and number-line graphs.
Adding or subtracting the same value preserves order; multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the order.
Compound inequalities combine conditions using “and” or “or.”
Contextual constraints may require whole-number, nonnegative, bounded, or otherwise restricted solutions.
unit.architecture: Open-age integrated Pre-Algebra learning: inequality meaning + number-line graphs + order preservation + negative reversal + multistep inequalities + compound inequalities + contextual constraints + discrete solutions + verification + mastery
unit.tool_integration: Calculator use is optional for arithmetic checks after students write the inequality, justify transformations, represent the solution set, and apply contextual constraints.
unit.readiness_note: Unit 09 develops inequality and constraint reasoning for learners of any age. Advancement is based on demonstrated mastery, not grade identity.

lessons.title: Inequality Meaning, Symbols & Solution Sets
objectives: Interpret <, >, ≤, and ≥ in words and contexts.
Distinguish an inequality from an equation.
Test whether a value belongs to a solution set.
Describe strict and inclusive boundaries.
warmup: Compare −4 and 2 using an inequality symbol.
Explain the difference between x<5 and x≤5.
Test whether 7 satisfies 2x+1>12.

concepts.heading: An inequality compares order
concepts.body: The symbols < and > show which value is smaller or larger; ≤ and ≥ include equality at the boundary.

concepts.heading: A solution set can contain many values
concepts.body: A value is a solution when substitution makes the inequality true. Most inequalities have infinitely many real-number solutions.

concepts.heading: The boundary may be included or excluded
concepts.body: A strict inequality excludes the boundary. An inclusive inequality includes it.

steps: Identify the variable a for age.
“At least” includes 18 and every greater value.

examples.answer: Yes, x=3 is in the solution set.
x≤−2 contains the boundary; x<−2 does not.

pathways.Foundation: Use symbol cards, verbal phrases, and true/false substitution tables.
pathways.Core: Move fluently among symbols, words, contexts, and tested values.
pathways.Extended: Analyze parameterized boundaries and distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions.

lessons.application: Find a public age, height, capacity, safety, eligibility, or measurement rule. Express it as an inequality and explain whether its boundary is included.

questions.explanation: At most includes 12 and smaller values.
An inequality contains an order-comparison symbol.

questions.prompt: A room holds no more than 80 people. If p is attendance:
questions.explanation: No more than means at most.

lessons.title: Number-Line Graphs & Interval Descriptions
objectives: Graph strict and inclusive inequalities on number lines.
Match symbols, words, and graphs.
Use open and closed points correctly.
Describe rays and bounded intervals informally.
warmup: Sketch x>2 on a number line.
What does a closed point at −1 communicate?
Describe all values between 3 and 8, including both endpoints.

concepts.heading: Open means excluded
concepts.body: Use an open point when the endpoint is not a solution, as with < or >.

concepts.heading: Closed means included
concepts.body: Use a closed point when equality is allowed, as with ≤ or ≥.

concepts.heading: Direction communicates order
concepts.body: Shade left for smaller values and right for larger values. Two boundaries create a bounded interval.

examples.problem: Write the graph open at 5 and shaded left.

examples.answer: All real values from −2 through, but not including, 4.

pathways.Foundation: Use floor number lines and endpoint cards before drawing symbols.
pathways.Core: Translate among symbolic, verbal, and graphical forms.
pathways.Extended: Compare interval notation, set-builder notation, and graph conventions.

lessons.application: Represent an acceptable temperature range, measurement tolerance, schedule window, or capacity interval on a number line.

questions.explanation: Values less than 6 lie to the left.

questions.prompt: Closed at 2 and shaded right represents:
Which value is not included in x<4?
questions.explanation: The strict boundary value is excluded.

lessons.title: One-Step Inequalities & Order Preservation
objectives: Solve inequalities using addition and subtraction.
Solve inequalities using positive multiplication and division.
Explain why order is preserved by these operations.
Check solutions and non-solutions.
warmup: Solve x+6<10.
Solve 5n≥35.
Choose a value that should satisfy p−4≤2.

concepts.heading: Undo the operation
concepts.body: Use inverse operations to isolate the variable, just as with equations.

concepts.heading: Positive scaling preserves order
concepts.body: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number keeps the inequality direction.

concepts.heading: Test values verify the set
concepts.body: Check a value inside the proposed solution set and one outside it.

pathways.Foundation: Use inverse-operation arrows and substitution checks.
pathways.Core: Solve and graph one-step inequalities fluently.
pathways.Extended: Justify order preservation with differences and number-line transformations.

lessons.application: Model a budget remaining after a fixed fee, a minimum score after an adjustment, or a maximum quantity per group.

lessons.title: Negative Multipliers & Reversing the Inequality
objectives: Reverse an inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Explain reversal using number-line order.
Solve inequalities with negative coefficients.
Detect common sign and direction errors.
warmup: Compare 2<5, then multiply both values by −1.
Solve −3x<12.
Explain why dividing by −4 changes direction.

concepts.heading: Negative scaling reflects the number line
concepts.body: Multiplying every value by a negative reflects positions across zero, reversing left-right order.

concepts.heading: The symbol reverses once
concepts.body: When the isolation step multiplies or divides by a negative, switch < with > or ≤ with ≥.

concepts.heading: Verification catches direction errors
concepts.body: Test one value from the claimed solution set in the original inequality.

pathways.Foundation: Use reflected number lines and color-coded reversal steps.
pathways.Core: Solve negative-coefficient inequalities and verify direction.
pathways.Extended: Prove reversal using ordered differences and analyze sign-unknown parameters.

lessons.application: Interpret a negative rate such as temperature decline, debt change, elevation loss, or reverse scoring without losing the order relationship.

options: negative scaling reflects order across zero
questions.explanation: Reflection across zero reverses left-right order.

questions.prompt: A student solves −3x<9 as x<−3. The error is:
questions.explanation: Division by a negative requires reversal.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Inequalities & Variables on Both Sides
objectives: Simplify and solve multi-step inequalities.
Use distribution and combine like terms.
Solve inequalities with variables on both sides.
Recognize all-real and empty solution sets.
warmup: Simplify 3(x−2)+4.
Solve 5x+1<2x+13.
Classify 2x+5<2x+9.

concepts.heading: Simplify before isolating
concepts.body: Distribute and combine like terms on each side before choosing inverse operations.

concepts.heading: Move variable terms strategically
concepts.body: Collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other, preserving order at each step.

concepts.heading: The variable may disappear
concepts.body: A true final statement means all allowed real values; a false statement means no solutions.

pathways.Foundation: Use a step organizer for distribution, combining, isolating, and graphing.
pathways.Core: Solve multi-step and both-sides inequalities with verification.
pathways.Extended: Analyze parameter cases producing bounded, empty, or universal sets.

lessons.application: Compare two pricing plans, production rules, or travel options and identify when one becomes less expensive or more efficient.

lessons.title: Compound Inequalities: “And,” “Or” & Intersections
objectives: Interpret compound inequalities using “and” and “or.”
Solve and graph intersections and unions.
Write chained inequalities.
Identify empty and overlapping compound sets.
warmup: Describe x>2 and x<7.
Describe x≤−3 or x≥4.
Which values satisfy both x≥0 and x<5?

concepts.heading: “And” means both conditions
concepts.body: The solution is the overlap, or intersection, of the two sets.

concepts.heading: “Or” means either condition
concepts.body: The solution is the union of values satisfying at least one condition.

concepts.heading: Chained notation compresses an interval
concepts.body: The statement −2≤x<5 combines two “and” conditions around the same variable.

pathways.Foundation: Use transparent number-line strips to see overlap and union.
pathways.Core: Solve, graph, and write compound inequalities.
pathways.Extended: Translate among set-builder, interval, and logical notation; analyze complements.

lessons.application: Model safe operating ranges, eligibility windows, acceptable dimensions, or schedules with multiple simultaneous conditions.

questions.explanation: The union has two separate rays.
No value is both greater than 7 and at most 7.

lessons.title: Contextual Constraints, Discrete Solutions & Verification
objectives: Write inequalities from real constraints.
Distinguish continuous and discrete solution sets.
Apply nonnegative, whole-number, and domain restrictions.
Verify solutions against mathematics and context.
warmup: Can a number of buses be 4.5? Explain.
Write a nonnegative constraint for time t.
A budget is $120 with a $15 fee and $8 items. What inequality models the item count?

concepts.heading: Context narrows the mathematical set
concepts.body: A solved inequality may allow all real values, while the situation permits only integers, nonnegative values, or a finite range.

concepts.heading: Discrete quantities are counted
concepts.body: People, tickets, buses, and packages usually require whole-number solutions.

concepts.heading: Verification includes units and feasibility
concepts.body: A correct symbolic value can still be impossible or unreasonable in context.

examples.problem: A $50 fee plus $12 per participant must stay at or below $230.
steps: Require p to be a nonnegative whole number.

examples.problem: At least 180 liters are needed. Each container holds 28 liters.
steps: Round up because containers are whole.

examples.problem: A walkway length satisfies 2.5≤L≤8, measured continuously.
examples.answer: Any real L from 2.5 through 8 is feasible.

pathways.Foundation: Underline limit words and label units before writing the inequality.
pathways.Core: Solve constraints and apply discrete or continuous domains.
pathways.Extended: Optimize within multiple constraints and critique hidden assumptions.

lessons.application: Design a budget, capacity plan, safety range, event schedule, environmental threshold, or production limit with explicit units and feasible solutions.

questions.prompt: A $20 fee plus $6 per item must be at most $80.
questions.explanation: Fixed fee plus per-item cost cannot exceed 80.

questions.prompt: The solution n≤10.5 counts people. Greatest feasible n:
questions.explanation: People require whole numbers not exceeding 10.5.

questions.prompt: Boxes hold 24 books. At least 130 books require:
questions.explanation: 130/24≈5.42, so six whole boxes are needed.

questions.prompt: Which contextual restriction is usually needed for elapsed time t?
A contextual answer should be checked for:
questions.explanation: Feasibility includes mathematical and contextual conditions.
